accroche: In 1847 in Vienna, washing hands with chlorinated lime drops mortality among women in childbirth from 18% to 2% in two months
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1847, at the general hospital in Vienna, a woman giving birth in the clinic run by physicians has a far greater chance of dying than if she gives birth a hundred meters away, in the clinic run by midwives. Neither team understands why.

## Two Clinics, Two Destinies

Ignaz Semmelweis has directed, since July 1846, the First Obstetrical Clinic of the Allgemeines Krankenhaus, where physicians and medical students work. A few meters away, the Second Clinic takes only midwives in training. In 1846, mortality from puerperal fever there reaches 11.4% in the first, against less than 3% in the second. The women themselves know it: some prefer to give birth in the street rather than be admitted to the physicians' clinic.

Semmelweis eliminates the received explanations one by one, climate, overcrowding, patients' modesty, without finding the decisive difference. It comes to him in March 1847, through a bereavement: his colleague Jakob Kolletschka dies of a generalized infection after cutting his finger during an autopsy. His autopsy reveals a pathology identical to that of the women who died in childbirth.

## Hands That Carry Death

Semmelweis then understands what no one had connected: the physicians and students of the First Clinic go directly from the autopsy room to the delivery room, with no precaution other than a cursory wash with soap and water. The midwives, for their part, never perform autopsies. It is not hands clean or dirty to the naked eye that matter: it is “cadaverous particles,” invisible, that soap does not remove.

In mid-May 1847, he imposes hand washing in a solution of chloride of lime before every examination. The effect is immediate: mortality in the First Clinic, which still reached 18.3% in April, falls to 2.2% in June, then 1.2% in July, finally matching the level of the midwives' clinic.

## Proof Without a Mechanism, Hence Without an Audience

Semmelweis cannot explain *why* chloride of lime works: the germ theory of disease, developed later by Pasteur and Koch, does not yet exist. Part of the medical profession therefore rejects his conclusion, which amounted to accusing the physicians themselves of killing their patients. Semmelweis responds with increasingly accusatory open letters, which does not help his cause. He dies in 1865, committed to an asylum, without having seen his method adopted on a large scale.

The shift lies in this gap: a practice can save lives even before its mechanism is understood, and the absence of an explanation is not a sufficient reason to ignore an effect measured so clearly. Hand washing, today a universal hospital reflex, took decades to stop being a marginal hypothesis.

repere.texte: Before mandatory hand washing, mortality from puerperal fever reached 18.3% in April 1847 in the clinic run by physicians. After its introduction in mid-May, it falls to 2.2% by June, then 1.2% in July.
repere.source: Ataman AD, Vatanoğlu-Lutz EE, Yıldırım G, “Medicine in stamps — Ignaz Semmelweis and Puerperal Fever,” Journal of the Turkish-German Gynecological Association, 14(1), 2013

carte.punch: Chloride of lime on the hands took one clinic's mortality from 18.3% to 2.2%.
carte.idee: In Vienna, Ignaz Semmelweis discovers that physicians unknowingly carry a deadly contamination from the autopsy room. Chloride of lime on the hands takes his clinic's mortality from 18.3% in April 1847 to 2.2% in June, before the germ theory.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Ignaz Phillip Semmelweis' studies of death in childbirth
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Detailed chronology of his career at the Vienna hospital.

quiz.question: Why did Semmelweis's theory take decades to be accepted, even though the effect of hand washing was measured so clearly?
choix: Because the mortality figures he put forward were disputed by his colleagues
Because the midwives refused to adopt the same method as the physicians
Because he could not explain by what mechanism chloride of lime acted
Because chloride of lime cost too much for routine hospital use
quiz.explication: The germ theory of disease did not yet exist: Semmelweis could show an effect, not explain it. His figures were not disputed, and neither the cost of the product nor the position of the midwives played any role in the rejection of his conclusion.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What triggers Semmelweis's decisive insight in March 1847?
choix: Reading an article on the germ theory of disease
The death of his colleague Jakob Kolletschka, infected after an injury during an autopsy
A surprise inspection by the Austrian health ministry
A midwife's account of her own hygiene methods
quiz_supplementaire.explication: In March 1847, his colleague Jakob Kolletschka dies of an infection after cutting his finger during an autopsy, and his autopsy reveals a pathology identical to that of the women who died in childbirth.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What becomes of Semmelweis at the end of his life?
choix: He receives a prize from the Vienna Academy of Sciences for his discovery
He changes specialty and becomes a military surgeon
He dies in 1865, committed to an asylum, without having seen his method adopted on a large scale
He emigrates to the United States, where his method is immediately adopted
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Semmelweis responds to critics with increasingly accusatory open letters, which does not help his cause, and dies in 1865, committed to an asylum, without having seen his method adopted on a large scale.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What distinguishes the practice of the physicians of the First Clinic from that of the midwives of the Second?
choix: The physicians go directly from the autopsy room to the delivery room, with no precaution other than a cursory wash
The physicians deliver a larger number of women per day
The midwives work only by day, the physicians at night too
The physicians use metal instruments, the midwives only their hands
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The physicians and students of the First Clinic go directly from the autopsy room to the delivery room with a simple wash in soap and water, whereas the midwives never perform autopsies.
